stories.author: sbulaev
stories.title: Why Large Language Models Fail at Tabular Prediction
stories.groq_label: Large Language Models (LLMs) fail at tabular prediction primarily because their accuracy decreases as data dimensionality grows, unlike classical baseline models which stay flat or improve.
stories.groq_discussion:
Discussion type: – Detailed:

This research focuses on why Large Language Models (LLMs) fail at tabular prediction. The Hacker News discussion suggests that commenters were primarily impressed by the study's approach, especially its use of a "purest inference regime" to evaluate LLM performance. At the same time, the discussion repeatedly highlighted concerns about the study's relevance to real-world use cases, with commenters debating issues such as the limitations of academic research and the need for more practical approaches.

One commentator noted that tree boosting is particularly effective for tabular data, which raises questions about whether LLMs are inherently flawed at this task or if it's just a matter of existing solutions being more well-suited. Another commentator observed that simply throwing an LLM at tabular data without proper tooling or scaffolding is not a viable approach, highlighting the importance of building a suitable harness to work with the data sensibly.

The overall impression was that the research introduces an interesting idea, but its long-term success depends on its relevance to real-world applications and its ability to address these criticisms.
stories.groq_explain: Large language models don't perform well when asked to make predictions about data lists or tables, and researchers have found that the reason is tied to the models' inability to handle a lot of data at once.
